title: The sower explained (Matthew 13:1–23)
hookLine: same words, different hearers: why one sentence sticks and another vanishes
tomorrow: what happens if you pull the weeds too soon?

cards: A whole podcast on the drive, and a week later one sentence is left. A teacher says a hundred things, and one of them follows you for years. Same speaker, same words, and some stick while the rest blow away.
Jesus told a story about exactly that, from a boat, to a crowd standing on the beach. A sower throws seed. Then he stops with one line: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear."

teach.b: Later he explains it. The seed is the same everywhere, and the sower throws it everywhere, even on the path. What changes is the ground.
The path is the one who "heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not," and it's snatched away. The stony ground takes it with joy, with no root, and trouble ends it.
Among the thorns, "the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word." Then the good ground: "he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit."
So the question is why words take root, and the answer is two verbs: hear, and understand, until it grows into something.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: NOT STUDY, BUT DEED.
teach.b: A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, a teacher named Shimon, son of Rabban Gamaliel, says in effect that the study isn't the main thing; the doing is.
Jewish and Christian teachers both say the hearing has to turn into a life.
And the honest difference: Pirkei Avot is speaking of Torah, God's teaching to Israel, studied and lived; Jesus' parable speaks of the word of the kingdom he is preaching.
One more thing in the parable: even the good ground yields some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. No contest. Only the question: is anything taking root?

how: Some Christians read a short passage slowly, more than once, and stop on one phrase to carry through the day, a practice called lectio divina; some Jewish communities study Pirkei Avot on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

practice: Write one sentence you've heard this week that you want to keep, by hand, on paper or a sticky note. Under it, write what it would look like done, one small thing, before tomorrow. Look at the two lines while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: The sower explained. Jesus' own reading of his story: one seed, four grounds, and the ground that understands bears fruit.

orig.note: Greek for understand, the verb in Matthew 13:19 and 13:23: hears the word, and understands it.

carryVoice: Your line: hear and understand. Then let it grow into something you do. Day done.
